planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline soil in part to full shade; Wester Flisk is a selected form of stinking hellebore prized for its red-flushed stems and flower nectaries, which contrast with the pale chartreuse bells and finely divided blue-green foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, since this selection is more heat- and drought-sensitive than plain-green stinking hellebore if sited in hot sun. Wester Flisk shows a distinctive red flush along its stems and around the rims of the pale chartreuse-green, bell-shaped flowers, set off by narrow, dark bluish-green divided foliage. It blooms in midwinter into early spring and self-seeds readily, though seedlings vary in how strongly they retain the red coloring, so division or purchase of named stock preserves the trait best. Cut back any tattered old flowering stems after seed set to tidy the clump.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade; Pacific Frost is a variegated sport of Corsican hellebore, discovered in a private garden in Vancouver, BC, with leaves heavily speckled and marbled in cream and gray-green.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, siting it out of harsh afternoon sun which can scorch the pale variegated patches on the leaves. Pacific Frost carries the same stout, three-lobed, spiny-edged leaves as the species, but each leaf is heavily mottled and speckled in cream and gray-green, making it a foliage standout even when not in bloom. Clusters of pale apple-green flowers open in late winter above the variegated foliage, and because the variegation does not come reliably from seed, the plant is propagated by division. Remove any leaves that revert to solid green to keep the clump's variegation strong.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall or early spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cinderella is a compact Gold Collection hybrid with glossy dark green foliage and nodding white flowers speckled pink and maroon.

directions: Set divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, where this compact hybrid resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Cinderella opens pale, near-white flowers speckled with pink and maroon in late winter, held above glossy, leathery, spine-edged dark green evergreen foliage. Like its Gold Collection relatives it is propagated by division or tissue culture rather than seed, and established clumps benefit from dividing every few years. Cut back old, weathered foliage in late winter just before the new flower stems emerge.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Champion is a vigorous Gold Collection hybrid with large flowers that open rosy-pink in bud, mature to creamy white with a pink blush, and held above sturdy, mottled evergreen foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving this vigorous hybrid room to form a substantial clump over time. Champion produces unusually large, outward-facing flowers that open rosy-pink in bud before maturing to a creamy white with a lingering pink blush, set against leathery, spine-toothed foliage marbled in gray-green. It flowers over a long season from midwinter into spring and, like other ericsmithii hybrids, is sterile and increased only by division. Remove old, weather-worn leaves in late winter so the flowers show clearly.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Candy Love is a Gold Collection niger x corsicus hybrid bearing upward-facing white flowers that develop a rose-pink blush toward the petal edges.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, where this hybrid combines the upright flower habit of Christmas rose with the sturdier, spinier foliage inherited from its Corsican parent. Candy Love bears outward- to upward-facing white flowers that deepen to a rose-pink blush along the petal margins as they age, appearing from late winter into spring above leathery dark green leaves. Being a sterile interspecific hybrid, it is propagated only by division or tissue culture. Thin or remove old foliage in late winter to let the flowers stand out against the fresh leaves.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Yellow Lady is a seed-strain selection of Lenten rose with nodding, soft butter-yellow flowers, often lightly freckled inside, that open in late winter.

directions: Plant in rich, humus-laden, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping the soil evenly moist while plants settle in. Yellow Lady bears nodding, cup-shaped flowers in a clear, soft yellow, sometimes lightly speckled inside near the nectaries, carried above leathery, dark green, palmate evergreen foliage. As a seed-grown selection rather than a clonal cultivar, individual plants show some variation in flower size and freckling, but all share the characteristic yellow coloring the strain was selected for. Remove old winter-damaged leaves just before bloom so the flowers show clearly against fresh foliage.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; White Lady is a seed-strain selection of Lenten rose with broad, pure white, outward-facing flowers that sometimes age to a pale green-white.

directions: Plant in rich, humus-laden, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, enriching heavy clay with compost before planting to improve drainage. White Lady produces broad, rounded, pure white flowers that face outward more than many Lenten rose seedlings and fade to a soft greenish-white with age, set above dark, leathery, evergreen palmate foliage. Being seed-raised, plants sold under this name vary somewhat in flower form, but all share the clean white coloring selected for in the strain. Deadheading is unnecessary for health, but cutting spent flower stalks after seed drop limits unwanted self-sown seedlings in beds where a tidier look is wanted.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Pippa's Purple is a named seed-strain selection with small, deep plum-purple flowers held well above the foliage on a compact plant.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where this compact selection forms a tidy clump smaller than many Lenten rose cultivars. Pippa's Purple carries small, rounded flowers of a deep, saturated plum-purple, held on sturdy stems that lift the blooms clearly above the dark evergreen foliage rather than nodding close to the ground. It flowers in late winter into early spring and, like other seed-strain selections, shows some plant-to-plant variation in exact shade and flower size. Remove tattered old leaves in late winter just before bloom to best display the deep-colored flowers.
